How Well Do Vision-Language Scene Graphs Serve
as Memory for Embodied Question Answering?

Divyansh Pandey* Email: divyanshpandey0108@gmail.com    Shubh Garg Email: divyansh@upailabs.org    Vedant Khandelwal Affiliation: Indian AI Research Organisation (IAIRO), GIFT City, Gujarat AI Institute, UofSC (AIISC), 1112 Greene St., Columbia Email: shubh.garg@iairo.ai    Niyati Rawal Affiliation: BITS Pilani *Equal contribution Email: shubhgarg265@gmail.com    Amit Sheth Email: kh.vedant02@gmail.com Email: niyati.rawal@iairo.ai Email: amit.sheth@iairo.ai Email: amitpsheth@gmail.com
Abstract

Embodied QA needs memory, but answer accuracy mixes retained evidence, reading errors and question priors. For a simulated multi-room scene-graph pipeline we define answerability: the fraction of questions a fixed rule-based reader answers correctly from the graph alone. The baseline recovers 24.1% of visible object types and its room labels flicker. Four targeted repairs double recall, raise answerability from 27.2% to 37.4%, and improve retrained QA from 71.4% to 75.9%, yet better object F1 can lower answerability. A question-type prior beats this reader on every predicted graph. In one real-video test, graph memory lowers accuracy. These exploratory findings favour scoring retained evidence alongside accuracy.

1 Introduction

An embodied assistant answering questions about a home must remember what it saw after leaving a room [10, 29, 48]. A common approach predicts each frame’s objects, relations and room as a scene graph, then lets a language model read the merged graph [39, 16, 44]. Final-answer accuracy mixes memory contents, the reader’s ability to use them, and question priors [42, 14]. A correct guess can conceal missing evidence; a reading error can conceal useful memory.

We audit a multi-room QA pipeline built on MomaGraph-R1 [21]. Its benchmark, baseline graphs, training recipe and no-memory/baseline QA runs are inherited (Supp. S1, S7, S11); our contribution is a diagnostic evaluation of memory evidence rather than a new memory method. We define answerability using a fixed rule-based reader, with abstentions counted as wrong. Four targeted repairs act as diagnostic interventions: higher object F1 can reduce question recovery, and better room continuity can hurt object–room queries (Figs. 1 and 2).

Related work.  Across interactive/photorealistic QA [13, 45], long-horizon memory [55, 19, 3], egocentric video [15] and situated 3D QA [5, 27], answer accuracy evaluates end performance. Question-prior controls [1, 8] motivate separating that score from retained visual evidence. Saha et al. [38] likewise score evidence selection apart from final answers; we score evidence retention.

Scene graphs encode building hierarchies [4, 36, 20], reconstructed objects [43] and open-vocabulary semantics [22, 28] for planning [33], navigation [53] and QA [2, 39]. Image memories retain another form of evidence [51, 34]; we examine what graph evidence supports before a trained task reader.

Image scene-graph generation [47, 54, 40] and panoptic graphs [50] target object/relation recovery using annotations such as Visual Genome [24]. Our fixed reader tests whether recovered content answers questions, connecting unanswerable-QA analysis [32] with scene-graph evaluation gaps [37]. Supp. S14 develops these distinctions.

2 Setting and protocol

Benchmark and dataset.  In each episode an agent in a ProcTHOR-10k house [11] (AI2-THOR [23]) walks from its spawn point to a target object in another room, through two to seven rooms of four types (Bathroom, Bedroom, Kitchen, LivingRoom). Each step stores a 256 px RGB frame, the agent’s room and the simulator’s visible-object record (type, instance ID and room of each visible object); episodes average 41.7 frames (10–116). Episodes are balanced over one, two, three and four or more door crossings. Templates write four multiple-choice questions per episode (two to four options; chance 33%) from the records of six sampled frames, the question strip. Eight types cover sequence queries (Order, Presence-change, Rooms-visited; 291 test questions) and set queries about objects and rooms (509; Tab. 1). Splits are house-disjoint: 5,000/500/200 episodes from 1,359/151/53 houses, with 800 questions and 8,335 frames on test. Supp. S11 gives dataset statistics and examples. Memory contains all frames except the last question-time view: 8,135 test frames.

Memory and QA.  MomaGraph-R1, based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B [41], predicts objects, relations and rooms (Fig. 2). A fixed renderer merges graphs into room-grouped text with visit order, first/last sightings, maximum simultaneous counts and relations. It drops walls, doors and floors, retaining at most 12 object types per room by sighting frequency and 24 relations per frame (Supp. S1). Graphs represent types, not tracked instances. MomaGraph-R1 is QA-trained with LoRA [18] for 6,000 optimiser steps, effective batch 16. Its answer-time image is blank; it reads the question, options and memory text. Training without memory supplies the question-only baseline. Runs share an auxiliary next-action objective and final-checkpoint evaluation (Supp. S7).

Protocol.  Simulator truth scores graphs and fits calibration/room naming on training/validation data. Only door segmentation additionally uses exact crossings; perfect rows use simulator graphs. A 300-test-frame prompt/resolution pilot informed development; test scores were visible during the conservative-calibration tie-break (Supp. S10). We therefore treat all test comparisons as exploratory. 95% confidence intervals (CIs) capture episode variability but not this selection effect: 20,000 paired bootstrap resamples of whole test episodes [12], averaging two QA seeds first.

3 Measuring retained evidence

Answerability.  A fixed reader applies Tab. 1 to the episodic graph and returns an option or abstains. Answerability is the fraction answered correctly; abstentions count as wrong. The rules have no learned prior, free parameters or test tuning. This scores graph recovery under specified rules; QA evaluates a trained reader of the rendered text. Object-type precision/recall/F1 compare predicted and visible types after benchmark-vocabulary name matching; room accuracy measures label correctness.

Reference graphs.  We separate room filing from temporal coverage using simulator-perfect graphs. Question strip, physical rooms: 97.5% (CI [96.4, 98.5]), with 100% on seven types and 82.8% on Rooms-visited. Memory frames, physical rooms: 80.4% [77.8, 83.0]. Memory frames, agent’s room: 59.9% [56.8, 63.1]. The 20.5-point filing cost arises when doorway sightings are assigned to the agent’s room rather than the object’s physical room. Extra memory frames can change counts and sighting times; room-type labels can merge distinct physical rooms. These constructions characterize the benchmark and reader, rather than universal memory bounds.

4 Diagnosis and targeted repairs

Baseline graphs miss objects and lose room continuity. Over all 8,335 test frames (including the last frames excluded from Tab. 2), object-type recall is 24.1%; small-object recall is only 8.3% even within 1.5 m. Of false positives, 57% are types absent from the entire episode. Room labels are correct in 45.5% of frames and switch 13.6 times per episode, versus 2.1 true label changes. Relation recall is 1.1%, and graphs lack the instance identities counting needs. Visual examples and the full breakdown are in Supp. S12.

Naming and hallucination errors recur systematically, consistent with object-hallucination studies in captioning and VLMs [35, 25]. The model often calls a dining table a Table or SideTable; six furniture types account for 61% of false positives. Requiring repeated sightings does not remove these persistent errors. These patterns motivate prompt redesign and per-type calibration, while room flicker motivates segment-level room decisions.

Fixes 1+2: resolution and prompting.  To recover small-object detail [46] and control naming, we re-render stored poses at 512 px and prompt with 106 types: the benchmark’s 104 plus Shelf and ShelvingUnit. Baseline graphs use 256 px frames and a prompt conditioned on the episode’s first question (graphs shared by its four questions) that lists only navigation structures outside the target room. The replacement drops both and requests all visible non-architectural objects, so it tests the prompt bundle, not vocabulary alone. In the 300-frame pilot, the prompt adds 16.0 recall points and higher resolution 12.3 more (Supp. Tab. S8). A post-hoc Grounding DINO [26] pilot scored below the VLM (Supp. S6).

Fix 3: per-type calibration.  We greedily fit keep/drop/rename rules to validation F0.5F_{0.5}, which weights precision above recall. The 28 rules rename Desk, Table and CoffeeTable to DiningTable and drop 25 types. A conservative variant uses validation answerability with a precision tie-break (Supp. S10); it retains the renames and drops only nine types with precision below 10%. Rules calibrate type decisions rather than confidence scores [17].

Fix 4: door-segmented rooms.  Following room-based geometric mapping [7, 20], consecutive agent door crossings delimit segments. Logistic regression names each segment from calibrated objects and VLM room votes, with training-data fitting and validation-selected regularisation. Repeated room types receive new numbers; these identify segments rather than physical-room revisits. A real agent would have to estimate these privileged crossings. Figure 2 locates the interventions; details are in Supp. S1–S3.

5 Results

Graph quality and usefulness.  The repairs double recall and raise answerability by +10.12 [+6.25, +14.00] points (Tab. 2); conservative calibration gains +12.62 [+8.38, +16.88]. Most of the gain precedes door segmentation: Fixes 1–3, without door segmentation, add +8.00 [+4.25, +11.75], or +10.50 [+6.62, +14.25] conservatively. Door segmentation gets the full-episode room count right in 199/200 episodes, versus 46/200 for baseline, but its overall answerability increment, +2.12 [−-0.88, +5.25], includes zero.

Precision can conflict with usefulness.  Calibration raises object F1 from 48.8 to 56.3 yet lowers answerability from 36.2 to 35.2. It removes types needed by Order questions, reducing that type’s score from 46.6 to 32.9; conservative calibration restores 42.5. Door segmentation also trades off tasks: Rooms-visited improves from 32.8 to 59.5, but Existence falls from 40.7 to 24.8 because agent-room filing creates ambiguous object–room assignments. Other types are in Supp. Tab. S3.

Sensitivity to door events.  Over 10 corruption seeds, timing offsets up to eight frames cost only 0.45 points. Missing or adding 10% of crossings lowers answerability to 36.1 or 35.6, respectively. At 25% errors, both fall below the image-only configuration (Supp. S5).

A memory-free prior.  The most frequent training answer value per question type scores 49.4%, exceeding every predicted graph read alone. Our reader abstains on 44.6% of questions; using the prior only on abstentions raises its score to 58.9%, versus 53.4% for baseline graphs with the same fallback. The paired gain remains +5.50 [+2.12, +8.88]. On Counting, always answering 2 scores 63.1%, whereas predicted graphs score only 5–11%. Missing objects and instance identities cost the reader most here.

Does better memory help QA?  Retraining on repaired graphs improves accuracy by +4.44 points (Tab. 3), concentrated in sequence questions (+11.17 [+6.68, +15.71]); set questions change by +0.59 [−-1.80, +2.96]. Test-time swaps give smaller gains, and perturbing memory lowers accuracy (Supp. S9.3, S13).

Real-video check.  On debiased VSI-Bench [49, 8] (2,362 questions, 274 ScanNet, ScanNet++ and ARKitScenes scans [9, 52, 6]), MomaGraph-R1 extracts graphs from 16 frames per scan at 640 px using the closed prompt and 65 question-vocabulary types. Qwen3-VL-8B [31] answers with official prompts/scoring, given identical frames in every frame-based condition. Adding memory reduces the score from 47.3 to 44.0, a paired scene-bootstrap change of −-3.32 [−-4.81, −-1.80] (Tab. 4). Counting falls from 46.5 to 35.3. Another scene’s memory scores 43.8, statistically indistinguishable from correct memory, so the loss may come from adding memory text rather than its content. Longer input, conflicting entries or unused graph content could each explain this (Supp. S8, S9.4). It uses one extractor and one answerer and omits Fixes 3+4, so it does not test the full pipeline.

6 Scope and conclusion

The reader is hand-written for eight templated question types, so free-form questions are untested; door segmentation uses simulator crossings; and since development saw test data, the gains need a pipeline frozen on training/validation data and scored once on unseen houses. Counting and room-assignment errors motivate instance identities and physical object locations in 3D. The real-video result motivates testing richer graph extractors and estimated room boundaries. Within these limits, better object F1 can still reduce question recovery: evaluating retained evidence reveals task trade-offs that recognition scores and answer accuracy alone conceal.

Supplementary Material

This supplement contains implementation details, additional diagnostics and analyses that extend the four-page paper. The main paper defines the reader, repairs and evaluation protocol and reports the central graph, QA and real-video results. Here S1–S3 give prompt excerpts and fitting details; S4–S6 add reader, corruption and detector diagnostics; S7–S10 document training and development; S11 adds benchmark and dataset statistics and examples; and S12–S14 give visual analysis, additional episode metrics and extended related work. Unless specified otherwise, intervals use the main paper’s paired episode-bootstrap protocol.

S1 Prompts and memory text

Baseline scene-graph prompt.  The baseline prompt is reproduced below, with long lines wrapped and dashes written as “–”; braces mark a slot that is filled in. The baseline graphs use this prompt, which follows MomaGraph-R1’s task-oriented format [21]. Its task instruction is the episode’s first question, given as context only.

You are an embodied robot perception system. Construct a scene
graph of ONLY the CURRENT image from visible evidence.
Building the scene graph is the task -- do NOT answer the
question.
Task instruction (context only -- do NOT answer it):
{task_instruction}
Reason first inside
<SCENE_GRAPH_ANALYSIS>...</SCENE_GRAPH_ANALYSIS>, then emit
exactly one JSON object inside
<SCENE_GRAPH_JSON>...</SCENE_GRAPH_JSON>.
STAGE 1 -- ROOMS (judge from the IMAGE, never from the
instruction text):
- scene_type: the room you are CURRENTLY IN, inferred from the
  visible objects/layout. Exactly one of: "Bathroom",
  "Bedroom", "Kitchen", "LivingRoom".
- target_scene: the room implied by the task instruction
  (where the target object lives). Same 4 values, or
  "unknown". This is the ONLY place the room named in the
  instruction may go -- it must NEVER set scene_type.
STAGE 2 -- OBJECTS (nodes): every object ACTUALLY VISIBLE now
(furniture, appliances, fixtures, doors, windows, decorations,
and navigation structures like door/hallway/entrance). Number
duplicates (chair1, chair2). Do NOT hallucinate hidden
objects. If scene_type != target_scene, the target object is
NOT in this room -- do NOT invent it; list only the visible
navigation structures (door/hallway/entrance) that could lead
out.
STAGE 3 -- EDGES: relationships between visible objects only,
using exactly these values:
- spatial_relationships: left_of, right_of, in_front_of,
  behind, higher_than, lower_than, close, far, touching
- functional_relationship: openorclose, adjust, control,
  providepower, activate, pairwith, support
- action_type: navigate, press, rotate, pull, push, open,
  close, insert, pick, release
- function_type: navigation, open_close_control,
  device_control, power_supply, water_flow_control,
  parameter_adjustment, special_function, assembly
Output EXACTLY (valid JSON only; do NOT answer the question):
<SCENE_GRAPH_ANALYSIS>
One short paragraph: which room you are in and the visible
objects that prove it, whether the target room differs (so
navigation is required), and the key visible
objects/relationships.
</SCENE_GRAPH_ANALYSIS>
<SCENE_GRAPH_JSON>
{"scene_type": "...", "target_scene": "...", "nodes": [...],
"edges": [{"object1": "...", "object2": "...",
"spatial_relationships": [...], "functional_relationship":
"...", "action_type": "...", "function_type": "...",
"is_touching": true}]}
</SCENE_GRAPH_JSON>

Closed-vocabulary prompt (Fix 2).  The object list and output schema are abbreviated in this excerpt:

You are an embodied robot perception system. List the objects
visible in this image.
STAGE 1 - ROOM: scene_type is the room you are CURRENTLY IN,
judged only from the image. Exactly one of: "Bathroom",
"Bedroom", "Kitchen", "LivingRoom".
STAGE 2 - OBJECTS: list EVERY object you can see, including
SMALL objects (cups, books, bottles, boxes, pillows, remote
controls, food, drawers, shelves) and objects in the background
or through doorways. Use ONLY these exact type names:
AlarmClock, Apple, ArmChair, ... [all 106 types] ... WineBottle
If an object matches none of these names, leave it out. Do NOT
list walls, floors, doors, windows or hallways. Number duplicates
(Chair1, Chair2). Do not invent hidden objects.
STAGE 3 - EDGES: spatial relationships between listed objects,
using exactly: left_of, right_of, in_front_of, behind,
higher_than, lower_than, close, far, touching.
[output format: <SCENE_GRAPH_ANALYSIS> one short paragraph,
then <SCENE_GRAPH_JSON> with scene_type, nodes, edges]

The ellipsis abbreviates the complete type list; it is not part of the extraction prompt.

Answer prompt.  Every QA model answers from this prompt, with a blank image (Sec. S7). The options are joined into one line (“A: 2 B: 3 C: 4”), and the model’s answer is the highest-scoring letter among the options the question offers.

### Task: Navigation has finished.
Answer the question using the memory collected during
navigation.
### Question: {question}
### Choices: {choices}
### Memory:
{memory text}
### Guidance:
Select the correct answer from the given options.
### Answer:

The no-memory model drops the two memory lines, and its second line reads “Answer the question using the visual information collected during navigation.”

Navigation prompt.  Training also includes an auxiliary next-action loss (Sec. S7). Its prompt pairs the current frame with that frame’s scene graph, written as three lines (ROOM, up to eight OBJECTS under their raw names, RELATIONS), with doors and walls kept:

### Task: Predict the next navigation action.
### Question: {question}
### Choices: {choices}
### Candidate Actions: (0) MoveAhead (1) RotateLeft
  (2) RotateRight (3) LookUp (4) LookDown (5) Done
### Predicted Scene Graph:
{current frame’s scene graph}
### Guidance:
Use the scene graph and the question to choose the best next
action.
Choose Done only when sufficient information has been
gathered to answer the question.
### Action Token: <CLS>

Memory text.  The memory text has this form:

ROOMS: {rooms in order of first visit}
VISITS (frames f0-f{N}): {room}@f{a}-f{b} -> {room}@f{c}-f{d}
  -> ...
{room}: {Type} x{n}[f{first}-f{last}],
  {Type}[f{first}-f{last}], ...
RELATIONS: {Type}-{relation}-{Type}; ...

Frame indices start at the episode’s beginning. Multiplicity is printed only when above one. Functional tags, when available, follow the frame interval, and repeated relations are listed once. Free-text names are mapped to the benchmark vocabulary before serialization.

S2 Calibration map

The conservative variant is called strict in the experiment logs and configurations. Table S1 gives the actual vocabulary edits, extending the main paper’s aggregate rule counts. Dropping a type removes every sighting of it. For Order questions, the number of undecidable cases attributable to dropped types rises from 7 to 19.

S3 Room-classifier features and fitting

The simulator’s leg index supplies the crossing events. For each object type, one feature is the fraction of a segment’s frames containing that calibrated type. Additional features are the fractions receiving each of the four VLM room votes or no vote. Training labels are the majority true room within each segment. Multinomial logistic regression is fit on 17,664 training segments; inverse regularisation is selected from {0.1,0.3,1,3,10,30}\{0.1,0.3,1,3,10,30\} by validation segment accuracy. The naming ablation and fit statistics are in Tab. S10.

S4 Additional reader diagnostics

Table S2 separates further abstention rates from incorrect decisions. Table S3 covers question types beyond the Order, Rooms-visited and Existence trade-offs quantified in the main paper. These are question-level breakdowns, rather than alternative definitions of answerability.

Scope of the reader.  The reader is hand-written for the benchmark’s eight templated question types (main paper, Tab. 1). Answerability therefore measures retained evidence for these question forms only. Free-form questions such as those in OpenEQA [29], or questions needing multi-step reasoning, have no matching rule, and we have not tested how the idea transfers to them. A transfer would need either a rule set per question family or a reader whose own errors can be measured separately from missing evidence.

Exact question-prior values.  The training modes are Order before, Presence-change yes, Rooms-visited 4, Persistence 1, Room ID bedroom, Existence painting, Counting 2 and Global count 4. These are answer values rather than option positions. If the value is not among a question’s options, the prior picks the most frequent correct letter for that type.

S5 Door-corruption implementation

Corruptions are applied before segment formation. Timing perturbations shift each crossing uniformly in [−k,k][-k,k] frames; each new segment takes the original segment label covering most of it. Missed crossings merge segments and retain the longer part’s label. Spurious crossings split a segment at a random interior frame, retain its label on both halves, and number the second as a new room. Crossing deletion uses probability pp per crossing; insertion uses probability pp per segment. Re-forming clean segments reproduces the uncorrupted construction.

For the main paper’s 10% perturbations, paired changes are −-1.29 [−-1.86, −-0.72] for missed crossings and −-1.82 [−-2.50, −-1.19] for spurious crossings. Conservative calibration with per-frame rooms scores 37.8 [34.5, 41.0].

S6 Detector threshold behaviour

Prompting eight classes together reduced Grounding DINO’s maximum score to 0.12, versus 0.30 for one class. Per-class thresholds were fit on 300 validation frames from 30 episodes. Validation F1 was 55.7, and 18 classes were switched off entirely, indicating overfit. A global threshold of 0.5 instead yielded F1 28.9. On the 300-frame pilot, Grounding DINO [26] with the validation-fit thresholds reached F1 45.9 versus 52.6 for MomaGraph-R1 with the closed prompt, at 10.7 versus about 0.65 s/frame. This comparison was run after the repairs were chosen. OWLv2 [30] was not tested. Table S5 adds precision and recall.

S7 Optimisation details

LoRA updates 88.8M of 8.38B parameters, including the vision encoder. Optimisation uses AdamW with learning rate 10−410^{-4}, cosine decay to 5% of peak, 5% warm-up, weight decay 0.01 and gradient clipping at 1.0. The micro-batch is one; arithmetic is bfloat16 and each run uses one H200 GPU. The navigation prompt in Sec. S1 supplies the auxiliary next-action classifier. Navigation performance is not evaluated.

S8 Real-video memory construction

Frames are spaced evenly through each scan and resized on the longest side. The text is inserted before the question as Memory of what you saw. Since scans lack room labels, the renderer omits rooms and lists per-frame objects together with first/last frame indices and maximum single-frame multiplicity. Each scene’s other-scene control is paired with a different scan. Despite the closed prompt, 37% of emitted names are outside the question vocabulary. The per-task results beyond the main paper’s counting and overall rows are in Tab. S12.

Why correct and unrelated memory score alike.  The answerer sees the same 16 frames in every frame-based condition, so memory text is the only difference. Correct memory scores 44.0 and another scene’s memory 43.8, both below frames alone (47.3). If the answerer drew on scene-specific graph content, correct memory should beat the unrelated control. That it does not suggests the loss comes from the presence of the memory text. Three causes fit this pattern and our runs cannot separate them. (i) The added text lengthens the input and may dilute attention to the frames. (ii) Memory entries can conflict with the frames: 37% of emitted names fall outside the question vocabulary, and the per-frame maximum count can undercount objects seen across frames, which is consistent with Counting falling from 46.5 to 35.3. (iii) The answerer may not use graph content at all. Memory alone scores 28.6, so the graphs carry some question-relevant content, but this run does not show whether the answerer reads it.

Scope.  This check uses one graph extractor and one answerer, and it omits calibration and door segmentation because scans have no room labels or door events. It tests the graph-to-answerer interface under these settings and does not evaluate the full repaired pipeline. Separating construction from use would need input-matched controls: filler text of the same length, the same graph with entries shuffled across objects, and a per-question check of whether the graph contains the answering evidence.

S9 Additional experiment records

Table S6 specifies the experiment bundle intended for anonymised review. It identifies the configurations, predictions and scripts needed to reproduce the results. The tables and plots below reproduce selected records; raw experiment assets are separate from the manuscript sources.

S9.1 Training trajectories

The repaired-memory models lead their baseline counterparts at all validation passes. No run’s most frequent predicted letter exceeds 49% of validation answers. Initial starts of the no-memory and baseline seed-0 runs were stopped before their first validation pass and restarted with identical arguments. The no-memory seeds answer 514 and 523 test questions correctly; the perfect-memory seeds answer 663 and 672. Both repaired-memory seeds improve on baseline memory: 608 and 606 correct, versus 572 and 571.

S9.2 Graph-generation and fitting records

A rerun of the original prompt reproduces stored-graph F1 closely (33.6 versus 32.6). Upscaling the same image adds 6.6 recall points without new detail; re-rendering adds another 5.7. This distinguishes model input size from newly resolved visual detail.

Validation F0.5F_{0.5} rises from 48.8 to 63.0 during greedy fitting, with precision moving from 48.2 to 67.4 and recall from 51.3 to 50.1. The first five rules provide half the gain. Table S9 resolves which categories drive false positives; Tab. S10 records the room-classifier fit.

S9.3 Memory substitutions without retraining

The substitutions preceded calibration. Removing false positives from the higher-resolution closed-prompt graphs improves QA by 2.00 points [+0.00, +4.00]; this diagnostic motivated calibration. With seed 0 alone, the perfect-graph swap gives +2.25 [−-0.25, +4.75]. Additional content/structure controls are in Tab. S18.

S9.4 Other real-video tasks and backbones

With identical frame inputs and decoding, MomaGraph-R1 scores 26.3 overall and its base Qwen2.5-VL-7B scores 26.2; InternVL3.5-8B scores 47.5. These backbone checks motivated the choice of answering model. Task-specific changes include −-5.6 for medium relative direction and −-5.3 for appearance order.

S10 Development details and visibility checks

Which choices saw test data.  Two development steps used test data. First, the 300-frame prompt and resolution pilot (Supp. Tab. S8) sampled test frames and ran while Fixes 1+2 were being chosen. Second, the conservative-calibration tie-break below was made with test numbers visible. All other fitting used training or validation data only: the full calibration map (validation F0.5F_{0.5}), the room classifier (training fit, validation-selected regularisation) and the reader rules, which have no fitted parameters. The paired bootstrap intervals describe variation over test episodes; they do not account for the choice of configurations, so the main-paper comparisons are exploratory. A confirmatory test would repeat the pilot on validation frames, freeze every choice, and score the frozen pipeline once on houses unused so far.

Conservative-selection tie.  Conservative calibration and renames-only tied at 36.5 validation answerability. The comparison printed validation and test numbers together; the tie was broken by validation precision while test results were visible. Renames-only scores 37.2 on test and conservative calibration 37.8. Conservative selection followed the starts of both full-calibration retraining runs, each taking about a day, so no conservative QA run was added.

Small objects needed by questions.  Visibility begins at about 6×66{\times}6 pixels in a stored frame. Only 31 test questions hinge on a small object never seen from closer than 3 m, distinguishing missed near-field evidence from questions requiring distant detail.

Provenance.  The experiment-order table distinguishes the inherited runs identified in the main paper from the subsequent graph diagnostics, simulator interventions, repairs and real-video tests.

S11 Benchmark and dataset details

This section adds statistics and examples to the main paper’s benchmark and dataset description. Test statistics are computed from the test episode records.

Episodes.  The reference route starts out of view of the target object instance and leads to it. The actions are MoveAhead by 0.25, 0.5 or 1.0 m, RotateLeft/RotateRight by 15, 30, 45 or 90∘, LookUp/LookDown by 15 or 30∘ within a pitch range of −30-30 to 60∘, and Done. Each step also stores the agent pose. All 200 test routes reach their target with these discrete actions alone. Figure S4 shows views from one episode outside the test split.

Visible-object record.  An object enters a frame’s record when AI2-THOR flags it visible within 6 m and its visible region covers at least 0.05% of the image (about 33 pixels), so partly occluded and cut-off objects count. The room in each entry is the room the object stands in, which can differ from the agent’s room when the object is seen through a doorway. Test frames contain 6.1 visible objects on average (median 5). A test episode shows 46.5 distinct object instances of 26.5 types on average, and 94 of the 106 types in the closed prompt (Fix 2) appear in test frames.

Questions and answers.  No language model writes questions or answers. Every gold answer is computed from the visible-object records and room labels of the question strip (Tab. S14). Answers therefore follow the strip even when a question’s wording refers to the whole run or house. Each question cites one to four strip frames, and its options are shuffled. The test split has 175 two-option, 245 three-option and 380 four-option questions (Fig. S3b).

Splits and route lengths.  The houses come from ProcTHOR-10k’s own training, validation and test partitions. A test house contributes one to five episodes (33 of the 53 contribute five). Each route stratum holds 50 test episodes (Tab. S13). Room labels name room types, so the 62 test routes that pass two rooms of the same type, including all of S4, contain two rooms with one label. Across test frames, 44% are in bedrooms and 17–21% in each of the other three room types; the target room is a bathroom in 89 of the 200 test episodes.

S12 Visual examples and additional error measurements

The frame-level illustrations expand the main paper’s teaser episode by showing raw predicted names before normalization. The aggregate panels resolve object type, distance and room confusion.

Small objects account for 35% of sightings. The benchmark vocabulary covers 94.5% of ground-truth mentions. Restricting correctness to objects physically within the agent’s room lowers baseline precision from 46.0% to 30.4%, quantifying how often visible objects belong to neighbouring rooms. Among the higher-resolution closed-prompt graphs, calibration reduces episode-absent false positives from 58% to 29%.

S13 Additional evaluation metrics and controls

Object–room recall measures whether a type is filed under its correct room. Order accuracy compares the relative first-sighting order of pairs of types. Route edit distance compares remembered and true room sequences; count error compares inferred counts with distinct simulator object identities. These episode-level measures complement the frame and question scores in the main paper.

The intermediate per-frame-room configurations count rooms correctly in 64/200 episodes. Even the simulator graph, when rooms share type labels, counts only 138/200 exactly: perfect perception does not supply a unique physical-room identity. The repaired graph’s remaining distinct-object count error is 1.08 and relation recall is 4.4%.

Another episode’s memory differs from the no-memory QA model by −-1.50 [−-4.00, +1.00], an interval including zero. This control probes useful episodic content rather than merely the presence of a memory field.

S14 Extended related-work distinctions

Task and observation scope.  Early EQA [10, 13, 45] couples answering to exploration, whereas OpenEQA [29] and episodic-memory benchmarks [48, 55, 19] emphasise retained observations. Ego4D [15] supplies egocentric video rather than a simulator’s object identities; ReMEmbR [3] places long-horizon memory in robot navigation. ScanQA and SQA3D [5, 27] instead query reconstructed spatial scenes. These observation regimes make different oracle constructions possible. Simulator identities permit our counting audit, while the real-video experiment can test utility without the same identity-based diagnosis.

What the representation preserves.  Hierarchical and dynamic scene graphs [4, 36, 20] distinguish structural levels such as rooms, places and objects; scan-level graph prediction supplies object relations [43]. ConceptGraphs, HOV-SG and Open3DSG [16, 44, 22] attach open-vocabulary semantics to spatial representations, and Clio [28] emphasises task-driven abstraction. Our frame-derived type lists do not inherit all of those geometric or identity properties. SayPlan, SG-Nav, GraphEQA and GraphPad [33, 53, 39, 2] illustrate how a downstream reader or planner can exploit a graph. Image-memory approaches [51, 34] retain another form of evidence; the present audit does not compare their full systems.

Metric and intervention scope.  Message-passing, motif-based, unbiased and panoptic scene-graph methods [47, 54, 40, 50] recover object/relation annotations such as Visual Genome [24]. The survey of 3D scene graphs [37] motivates examining downstream use beyond annotation matching. Question-prior studies [42, 14, 1, 8] explain why this requires explicit controls. The relation to unanswerable reading comprehension [32] concerns missing evidence under a specified question/reader pairing, rather than a guarantee that another reader cannot answer. New Evidence, Same Choice [38] also scores an intermediate evidence decision apart from the final answer: a vision-language model sees a physical measurement and must either answer or pick the cheapest experiment that resolves the question, and endpoint accuracy hides failures to switch that choice. The two diagnostics sit at different points. Theirs asks whether a model selects the evidence a decision needs; answerability asks whether memory still holds sufficient evidence before any reader acts. A memory can retain the evidence while a reader fails to select it, which is one reading of our real-video result.

The repair choices connect to separate research threads: hallucination diagnostics [35, 25], high-resolution visual search [46], type-decision calibration rather than calibrated probabilities [17], geometric room segmentation [7], and open-set detectors [26, 30]. The controlled audit keeps the extractor fixed rather than attributing these threads’ full capabilities to the repair pipeline.
